article_text:
Eigentlich ist Regisseur Robert Eggers im Oktober 2026 vor allem in Sitges, um beim dortigen Festival des fantastischen Films seinen „Premio Máquina del Tiempo“ abzuholen, einen Preis fürs bisherige Lebenswerk für Filmschaffende, die eigentlich noch zu jung für große Karriere-Rückblicke sind. Neben Dankesreden hat der 43-jährige New Yorker mit „ The Witch “ jenen Film mitgebracht, mit dem er 2015 hier an der spanischen Mittelmeerküste das erste Mal reüssierte: Das frisch in Bild und Ton restaurierte Werk wird dem Publikum des katalonischen Festivals auch als Dank für die langjährige Gastfreundschaft präsentiert. Doch Eggers bringt auch noch eine ganz besondere Zugabe nach Sitges mit: die ersten acht Minuten seiner mit Spannung erwarteten Aufarbeitung des Werwolf-Mythos, „ Werwulf “, die zu Weihnachten in den USA und im Januar 2027 in die deutschen Kinos kommen wird.

Weit weg vom Mainstream-Look

Der zusammenhängende Clip aus der Mitte des Films zeigt eindrücklich, wie ernst es Eggers mit seinen archaischen Bilderwelten ist. Es sei sein am konsequentesten durchkomponierter Film, meint Eggers bei der Präsentation der Szene, in der Willem Dafoe als Werwolfjäger mit den abscheulichen Taten eines neuen Kombattanten vertraut gemacht wird. In der Tat. Wirkten schon die entsättigten Bilder seines restaurierten Hexenfilms von 2015 wie ein Fluch aus einer menschenfeindlichen Zeit, ist das Mittelalter um 1305 in Britannien, in dem „Werwulf“ spielt, noch einmal grauer, unwirklicher und gottloser.

Hinzukommt, dass das an Stummfilme erinnernde „Academy-Format“ (ein in CinemaScope-Zeiten selten gebrauchtes Bildformat im fast quadratischen Verhältnis von 1.37:1) sowie die aschgrauen, an alte Tusch-Lavierungen von Alfred Kubin erinnernden Bilderwelten den Film formal weit weg vom herkömmlichen, brillantscharfen Mainstream-Look entfernen.

„Es in der Tat mein absolut düsterster Film“

Und inhaltlich? „Eigentlich mag ich die Geschichte lieber als den Horror …“, meint Eggers in Sitges, „…und um ehrlich zu sein, hätte ich ‚Werwulf‘ der Authentizität wegen im Deutschland oder Frankreich der Zeit spielen lassen müssen und nicht in England um 1305. Aber ich wollte dieses Spätmittelalter besonders krude und archaisch erscheinen lassen, und da sind mir diese Aufzeichnungen der Werwolf-Tötungen in Britannien zupassgekommen. Willem Dafoes ‚Alter Jäger‘ beruht ja auf einem Charakter, den es wirklich gegeben hat.“ All das verleiht „Werwulf“ eine atemberaubende Aura. „Es in der Tat mein absolut düsterster Film, und mir wurde selbst manchmal schlecht bei dem Gedanken, was ich mir da beim Drehbuchschreiben habe einfallen lassen, aber ich hoffe, dass Sie dennoch an meiner Welt Gefallen finden.“ Der Ton ist in jedem Fall gesetzt.

article_text:
Trump Administration

DC Protesters Slam Trump's Fascist Triumphal Arch

A group of 50 used puppets and a fake arch to deliver the point that Americans are against the "Arc de Trump."

Hyperallergic )

WASHINGTON, DC — South of Memorial Circle, within eyeshot of the Lincoln Memorial and John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, more than 50 protesters gathered yesterday, November 5, to oppose Trump’s proposed 250-foot Triumphal Arch ahead of the National Capital Planning Commission’s (NCPC) final meeting to vote on the project.

Hours after the NCPC approved the arch in an 8–4 vote, a district court judge granted the District of Columbia and Virginia a 14-day restraining order to halt construction .

At the event organized by Third Act DC, an environmental and pro-democracy action group for area residents aged 60 and up, two Virginia Congressional representatives, an Arlington County Board member, and Greg Werkheiser, an attorney with Cultural Heritage Partners, spoke about how the arch would infringe on the architectural and spiritual purpose of the space. He was one of two people associated with lawsuits that the District of Columbia and Virginia , the Arlington County Board , as well as Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian filed against the National Park Service and Department of the Interior in opposition to the arch.

article_text:
Unspoken emotional wounds linger throughout “ Between Us ,” Japanese director Matsumura Shingo’s new film playing in the Tokyo International Film Festival ’s Nippon Cinema Now section, its strand for Japanese films.

The film follows Makoto and Kasumi, childhood best friends who drift apart after an incident on a joint family camping trip and reunite six years later in their high school drama club. Kawashima Ririka, Kurasawa Anna, Kikuchi Akiko, Usuda Asami, Saito Yoichiro and Miura Takahiro star. The script leaves a lot unsaid, letting patient camerawork absorb the emotional information each character tries to withhold.

Ted Sarandos Addresses Netflix Content Exec Purge: 'I Know That We Could Do Better'

Matsumura, whose credits include “The Lump in My Heart” (2023), favors very still camera movement and deliberate observation. He has set himself a rule against using handheld camerawork in his films.

“All the cameras are becoming all compact right now, and you see all these videos shown on YouTube and social media that are shot by those cameras,” he says. “And so I wanted to differentiate what I show on the big screen with that kind of content. That is one of the reasons why. The second reason is that I want to capture the emotion of the actors truthfully, slowly.”

There’s a fascinating contrast in how “Between Us” seeks emotional realism but finds it through very measured, precise camerawork, particularly in how it turns the emotional distance between Makoto and Kasumi into literal distance through the blocking of each scene.

“What was more difficult to portray was [that] though they are apart, they are feeling the existence of the other,” Matsumura says, “and I wanted to show that with the use of the eyes and use of the space: though there was a physical space [between them], they kind of had each other in mind, and I wanted to express that through other elements.”

The drama club has lost members because Kasumi takes it so seriously that others feel they can’t keep up. Even after Makoto joins the club, the two are often shot far apart, but Matsumura shows the mending through a rather simple editing decision: cutting the girls’ separate read-throughs as though they are trading lines, with each cut bringing them closer than ever before, even though they aren’t in the same room.

“The play is a fiction, but they are speaking in their own language,” he says. “And by saying their lines, they are able to say what they were not able to say in the real world, and by doing that, their distance becomes closer.”

The script Kasumi discovers, which gives the film its title, becomes what begins to mend their relationship, quite literally bringing them closer together.

The intimate story has big-picture beginnings. Matsumura found inspiration in a run of disasters, starting with the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake.

“There was the pandemic. There is the war going on around the world, and [it] was a period in my life when I thought it is impossible for one to connect with others,” he says. “So I just wanted to make a very simple film with two people, two human beings facing the other way, and to make them look at each other, and [ask] what kind of energy is born from that?”

The story has nothing to do with those events in a literal sense, Matsumura says. What ties them to the past trauma linking Makoto and Kasumi’s families is that both are “unresolved.”

“I think that reflects the current situation where the earthquake, the nuclear power plant, the war, if it’s on the media, we look into it. But once it’s not on the news, we feel that it’s kind of in the past solved, but it’s really not in reality,” he says.

With his two leads, “there was no specific direction that I gave them,” Matsumura says. “This is a characteristic that they have as an actress – it’s a common characteristic – but they have interest in others, and they listen to others closely, and they take in their words and make it their own, and they have this trait. It was very natural for them to actually perform these two characters, and I just let them freely perform what they felt like.”

Matsumura’s visually organized approach, paired with naturalistic performances, makes for a striking result, one that also shows the range of styles across this year’s Nippon Cinema Now lineup.

“There is really no [singular] mainstream in the Japanese cinema now,” Matsumura says. “But one thing that is common is that the financing, the budget that we have for one film is very limited in Japan – it’s not like in the U.S. And because of that, there is a limit to what we can portray, the concept that we can portray in one film.”

That isn’t always a negative thing, he adds. “We are all trying to make a film about a subject that is within our reach, but we’re not reaching for all the same things. We’re reaching for all different things, and that is the current Japanese cinema environment. So we’re not making a film about one big subject. Each of us are all making films about [a] variety of small subjects.”

Matsumura says he is at a crossroads himself. “I could follow my instinct and make an artistic film, and express what is inside of me, or I could make a film for the mass audience – I won’t be facing with myself, but I’ll be facing more towards society or the audience that watches the film,” he says. “I don’t know which way I’ll go, as of now.”

article_text:
U.K. audiences aren’t usually ones to give standing ovations. But when one of their most cherished filmmakers makes a final bow, unwritten rules are allowed to be broken.

This was certainly the case for Mike Leigh , who on Thursday received a hero’s welcome at the London Film Festival premiere of “ Tender Loving Care ,” a film he’s said will likely be his last.

The director — an icon of British cinema for decades with a celebrated body of work that includes “Secrets & Lies,” “Naked,” “Vera Drake” (which opened the 2004 London Film Festival), “Happy-Go-Lucky” and “Topsy-Turvey” — walked onto to the stage ahead of the screening to applause, cheers and, after a few seconds, with almost the entire room at London’s Royal Festival Hall rising to their feet in appreciation.

When the clapping died down, the director responded, in typical Leigh style, with: “You haven’t even seen it yet.”

Starring Kate O’Flynn, Marion Bailey and Paul Jesson, “Tender Loving Care” — set and shot in London — explores themes of aging, grief and relationships, while casting a harsh light on the underfunded British health and welfare system. The film premiered at Telluride and won both the top prize at the San Sebastian Film Festival and best leading actor award for O’Flynn.

Speaking via video in San Sebastian and echoing comments he’d made earlier, Leigh said the film was “more than likely” his final film due to his own health issues. “It’s quite straightforward, I have a medical condition [myositis], which affects my muscular movement, and it’s quite difficult to move around,” he said. “[It’s] certainly more difficult than it should be for a filmmaker, and therefore it’s more than probable that this film will have to be my last film. That’s all.”

He added: “It’s a practical matter to do with my medical condition — a physical condition.”

Leigh has a long history with the London Film Festival, with many of his films have screened there. Alongside titles such as “Another Year,” “Peterloo,” “Naked,” “Vera Drake,” “Life Is Sweet” (which had its world premiere at LFF in 1990), “Mr. Turner” and last year’s “Hard Truths,” Leigh brought his very first feature, “Bleak Moments,” to the festival in 1971.

article_text:
“The Dropout,” Hulu’s 2022 limited series in which Amanda Seyfried plays Elizabeth Holmes , has seen a massive audience spike due to the buzz surrounding A24’s new Holmes documentary “ You Can See Everything .”

Viewership of “The Dropout” jumped by 186% in September compared to the month before, driven by the Sept. 6 announcement that “You Can See Everything” had been produced in secret. That interest continued growing as the film’s Oct. 16 wide release approached, with viewership during the week of Oct. 12 increasing 92% compared to the week before.

Related Stories

Cynthia Erivo Says ‘Not Enough Credit Is Given to Intimacy Coordinators’: ‘They’re Often Given a Hard Time’ but ‘What They Do Is Important’

James Austin Johnson's Trump Stops by 'SNL U.K.' for Meeting With Burnham and Zelenskyy: 'You Don't Have One Guy Who Can Play Trump?'

The data remains impressive when looking at specific totals: In August, before the buzz around “You Can See Everything” began, “The Dropout” was watched for 420,000 hours (or roughly 62,000 views when divided by the series’ nearly seven-hour runtime) — already decent for a four-year-old series. In September, viewership skyrocketed to 1.2 million hours, or 176,000 estimated views. The week of Oct. 12 alone brought in another 422,000 hours watched or 62,000 views; in other words, “The Dropout” brought in as many eyes during that seven-day period as it did in the entire month of August.

Interest remains high now that the film is in theaters: “The Dropout” has reached 997,000 hours watched (148,000 views) to date this month, bringing the total since September to 2.2 million hours, or 296,000 estimated views.

JustWatch, a service that centralizes information about where various streaming programs are available, also reported increased interest in “The Dropout.” The series jumped 200% in search points week-over-week after the release of “You Can See Everything,” and is in the No. 10 position on the site’s current streaming search rankings.

“The Dropout” isn’t the only piece of Holmes media enjoying a bump thanks to the success of “You Can See Everything”: John Carreyrou, the journalist who brought down Holmes’ fraudulent empire, returned to the New York Times bestseller list with his 2018 book “Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup.”

Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, “You Can See Everything” premiered as a surprise screening during the Telluride Film Festival, before which its existence had not been made public.

“The Dropout” was created by Elizabeth Meriwether and was widely loved upon its 2022 release, with Seyfried winning the Emmy for lead actress in a limited series. That year, Meriwether and Seyfried both indicated to Variety that they would be interested in making another project about Holmes — “I’m not kidding, a two hour special!” Seyfried said — though Seyfried was more reticent in a recent interview.

2027年1月16日〜2月21日に札幌市内11会場を中心に開催される「札幌国際芸術祭2027（SIAF2027）」の全参加アーティスト34組、および各会場コンセプトや展示詳細、夜間プログラムなどが公開された。

札幌の街を「雪の惑星」に見立て、「PLANET SNOW（プラネット・スノー）—upas mintar / upas nociw（ウパㇱ ミンタㇻ / ウパㇱ ノチウ）」をテーマに据える本芸術祭では、11会場にはそれぞれ「情報館」「博物館」「地下道」「学校」など、惑星における役割が与えられる。都市の日常的な機能や施設が、「プラネット・スノーに存在する施設」へと姿を変える構成だ。

ディレクターチームの 小川秀明 、 細川麻沙美 、 漆崇博 、 丸田知明 は、 「アートと多様な領域との『掛け算』を原動力に、雪を起点に地球を越え、宇宙にまで想像を広げる」 とコメント。会場では、人類の歴史を語る巨大なロボット、未来から人間の本質を問いかけるアンドロイド、過酷な自然環境から着想したオートクチュール、流木や獣の骨から生まれた生き物、雪の広場に現れる光を放つ岩など、多彩な作品に出会える。

日中に巡ることができる会場

札幌文化芸術交流センター SCARTS では、ソニーグループによる没入型インスタレーション《OPTICAL DRIFT》が世界初公開される。札幌市民ギャラリーには、北海道津別町にある造形作家・大西重成による私設美術館「シゲチャンランド」が出張展示。ノルウェーのアーティスト、フローデ・オルデレイド＆トーマス・クヴァムによる高さ約4mの巨大な銀色のロボット《Requiem for an Exit》も登場する。

北海道博物館では、石黒浩／いのちの未来研究所によるアンドロイド《ヤマトロイド》が、館内を巡りながら「人間とは何か」を問いかける。 モエレ沼公園 には、ファッションデザイナー・中里唯馬のコレクション《GLACIER》が国内初公開。過酷な自然環境に着想したオートクチュールが、雪原のガラスのピラミッドに並ぶ。の中央区複合庁舎では、絵本「100かいだてのいえ」の作者・いわいとしお（岩井俊雄）が、「雪の100かいだてのいえ」をつくるワークショップを開く。札幌大通地下ギャラリー 500m美術館では、公募で選ばれた大西康明と鈴木悠哉が、それぞれ全長48mの作品を展示。 北海道立近代美術館 では、コレクションから雪の表現を集めた展覧会「雪々と」を開催する。このほか、札幌市青少年科学館、 札幌市資料館 （旧札幌控訴院庁舎）でも、体験型の作品が展開される。

夜まで楽しめるプログラムも

さっぽろ雪まつり大通会場（2月4日〜21日、大通公園西2丁目）には、アート＆テクノロジースタジオ・ENESSの大規模インスタレーション《IWAGUMI Air Scape》が登場する。高さ最大14mの岩型バルーン群が、日建設計による会場デザインとともに、雪まつりの景観を一変させる。AOAO SAPPORO（1月9日〜2月21日）では、《IWAGUMI Air Scape》の着想源となった「ネイチャーアクアリウム」の常設展示に加え、ENESSの作品も特別に登場する。あわせて、冬の恒例イベント「さっぽろホワイトイルミネーション」にもSIAFがディレクションで参加する。中島公園会場（1月9日〜28日）には、ENESSの最新作《SNOWFISH》が世界初公開される。

このほか、夜まで楽しめるプログラムとして、札幌市資料館（旧札幌控訴院庁舎）の壁面に、アーティストによる映像プロジェクションを夕方に実施。新札幌地区では、栗林隆の体験型作品《元気炉》も展開される。

会期初日の1月16日には、音楽家・大友良英と北海道ビッグバンドによるオープニングライブを札幌近松で開催。会期を通して、トークやワークショップなどのイベントが予定されている。また、来場者が各会場を巡るためのガイドブック「プラネット・スノー フィールドガイド」も準備されている。アドバイザーには、宇宙飛行士の山崎直子が名を連ねる。

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Rome Flynn ( Godfather of Harlem , How to Get Away With Murder) has joined the cast of Throttled , Amazon MGM Studios ‘ new romance film based on the first book in Lauren Asher’s bestselling Dirty Air series.

From screenwriter Melissa Osborne and director Nzingha Stewart, Throttled stars Nicole Wallace as Maya Alatorre, an ambitious young woman who joins her brother on the racing circuit and falls into a forbidden, high-stakes romance with her brother’s ruthless teammate and fiercest racing rival, Noah Slade (Josh Heuston). Julio Peña will play Santi Alatorre, Maya’s older brother and a driver on the racing circuit. Mia McKenna-Bruce will play Sophie, Maya’s best friend.

Flynn will portray Jax Kingston, a highly skilled and competitive driver for Team McCoy who shares a particularly tense rivalry with Noah Slade, sources close to production tell Deadline.

Watch on Deadline

Max Handelman and Elizabeth Banks of Brownstone Productions are producing alongside Ethea Entertainment’s Jennifer Gibgot and Andrew Panay, with Garret Grant also producing. Alison Small of Brownstone Productions and Lauren Asher are executive producing.

Flynn’s most recent projects include Apple TV+’s Imperfect Women, playing Kerry Washington’s love interest, Jordan, and the four-episode anthology series Side Quest , a spinoff of Mythic Quest expanding on how games affect people in different ways. He can currently be seen as Frank Lucas (previously portrayed by Denzel Washington in American Gangster ) in MGM+’s fourth season of Godfather of Harlem, opposite Forest Whitaker. Flynn is repped by Artium Talent and Weiner Management.

article_text:
Sacha Baron Cohen opened up about his experience signing on to play the demon Mephisto in the Marvel Cinematic Universe during a live “Happy Sad Confused” conversation at New York’s 92nd Street Y. The actor, currently on tour promoting “Ali G: Who Iz I?,” recalled how the creative team working on last year’s Disney+ series “ Ironheart ” took an extra careful approach when pitching him the idea of playing a character representing the devil.

“It was a wonderful meeting when I was offered it,” Baron Cohen told Josh Horowitz Wednesday night. “It was primarily, I think, an almost entirely Black producing and directing team. And they said, ‘We want to offer you Mephisto, but we are aware of the negative association of Jews historically with the devil, and we want to make sure that you’re not insulted by us offering this.’ It was such an amazingly considerate, empathetic thing to say. And I was like, ‘Yeah, I’m good.’”

Stereotypes associating Jewish people with horns and other demonic characteristics stem from a centuries-old mistranslation of the Bible, which helped perpetuate the antisemitic myth. “Since medieval times,” the Brandeis Center writes, “Jewry has frequently been depicted as a wealthy, powerful, menacing and controlling collectivity, demanding the sacrifice of others to their own greed.”

Mephisto, inspired by the devil-like figure Mephistopheles, has a reputation in Marvel comics for tricking superheroes into making deals with him, often in exchange for their souls. And in the series finale of “Ironheart,” Dominique Thorne’s Riri Williams strikes a deal with Baron Cohen’s Mephisto to bring her deceased best friend back from the dead.

“I think for the Jews out there, sometimes we don’t feel seen,” Baron Cohen explained. “We don’t feel like people can empathize with us, that we are suffering too. And so to have this entirely Black producing and directing team be so empathetic, was a moment of being seen. It was an amazing experience.”

“Ironheart” was created by Chinaka Hodge, with “Black Panther” director Ryan Coogler and Zinzi Coogler among its executive producers.

Marvel Studios did not immediately respond to Variety’s request for comment.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "好莱坞万人迷一向以高颜值和个人魅力闻名。但在一次经典的剧情反转中，最近让观众们心猿意马的大银幕梦中情人甚至都不是人类。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在浪漫喜剧片《Wicker》中，亚历山大·斯卡斯加德（Alexander Skarsgård）饰演的“柳条丈夫”（Wicker Husband）角色在互联网上引发了狂热。", "links": [{"text": "the romcom Wicker", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/30/i-saw-the-script-and-went-oooh-olivia-colman-and-alexander-skarsgard-on-their-steamy-folk-horror-movie-wicker"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“再也不能直视我的庭院家具了，”一条Instagram评论写道。宜家（Ikea）在其藤编家具的照片配文中用了“丈夫人选”（husband material）一词。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，藤编社群却因为截然不同的原因而激动不已。“柳条丈夫”不是用柳条制作的，而且他看起来像是被编结（plaited）而不是编织（woven）出来的，这一事实惹恼了一些手艺人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/09cca9caafc5dbf003f61c9d07f5912ff5f41927/0_0_8256_5504/master/8256.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Olivia Colman’s Fisherwoman embraces Alexander Skarsgård’s beast-faced Wicker Husband outdoors", "caption": "Alexander Skarsgård as the Wicker Husband and Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman. Photograph: Black Bear/PA", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "黛博拉·尼德曼（Deborah Needleman）曾任《纽约时报》旗下《T》杂志编辑，后来转型成为编篮手艺人，她是较早对此提出质疑的人之一。她在Instagram上写道：“我很高兴编篮社群现在有了属于我们自己的性感、由藤条编织的男主角，但我也有疑问。为什么一个在英国渔村里编织出来的家伙不是用柳条——甚至连灯芯草都不是？！”此后，已有100多位同行编篮手艺人发表了看法。", "links": [{"text": "Instagram", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/deborahneedleman/p/Db1iGmuj95Y/?hl=en"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《牛津英语词典》将柳条（wicker）定义为“扭绞在一起用于制作篮子、家具等的细木条”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "伦敦编篮工会（Worshipful Company of Basketmakers）的行业顾问埃莉诺·摩根（Eleanor Morgan）表示，虽然柳条过去常用来指代藤编，但如今它的受欢迎程度已有所下降。“历史上，藤编可以指任何柔韧的嫩枝或柳条，”她说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "维塔工作室（Wētā Workshop）是新西兰的特效工作室，曾负责制作“柳条丈夫”的上半身。该工作室的道具设计师乔·邓克利（Joe Dunckley）表示，为这样一个有感知能力却由柳条构成的角色制作戏服是一项“巨大的挑战”。“大多数道具材料都很柔软以模仿皮肤。但他并非血肉之躯。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了呈现藤编效果，邓克利和他的80名专家团队为斯卡斯加德制作了50个互锁的车身部件以供穿着。他们利用类似橡胶的热塑性弹性体，3D打印了由该工作室编写代码的定制编织层，然后将其固定在氨纶紧身衣上。在历时18个月的过程中，他们还制作了10款面部假体。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/47a8d57e0c4910f0a240d1f589bc380db565bace/0_0_6000_4000/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "A closeup of hands painting a detailed woven limb with a small brush", "caption": "An artisan creates a limb of the Wicker Husband at the Wētā workshop in New Zealand. Photograph: PR Handout", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "邓克利表示，对于他们对这套戏服的功能需求而言，柳条并非一个可行的选项。“这背后的原因类似于为什么在电影中我们不用真正的钢铁制作盔甲，也不使用真正的宝剑。这是一部奇幻电影。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "来自加的夫的编篮手艺人刘易斯·普罗瑟（Lewis Prosser）表示，每个手艺人都在思考自己会如何应对这项任务。“这肯定不是我会采用的方式，但这并不意味着它不好，”他说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "普罗瑟表示，他对藤编的理解是“一种被编织出来的物体，但它明确不是纺织品”，并补充道“有些人会不同意我的看法”。包括尼德曼在内的一些编篮手艺人则认为，藤编指的是一种编织类型，而不是某种材料。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "after newsletter promotion", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于采用威尔士和英格兰西南部传统技艺制作藤编戏服的普罗瑟来说，制作篮子主要有3种方法。盘绕法（coiling，将植物材料的纤维以螺旋状缠绕在一起）、辫织法，或者立柱及支架篮艺（stake and stand basketry，即通过水平线材编织垂直杆）。“我们传统上称为‘藤编物品’的通常会具备后一种特点，”普罗瑟说。“柳条丈夫”则没有。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管片中的演员奥利维亚·科尔曼（Olivia Colman）和村民们说的是各种英国方言，但该片的故事背景并非设定在英国。邓克利透露，彼特·丁拉基（Peter Dinklage）饰演的编篮手艺人角色曾游历世界，向其他手艺人学习了各种手艺。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/28462413884a7e05f6ba35f83e01e355d9a3b371/0_0_5472_3648/master/5472.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Wētā Workshop’s lead weaver Jasmin van Lith weaves a small intricate object in a cluttered studio", "caption": "Lead weaver Jasmin van Lith at the Wētā workshop. Photograph: PR Handout", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "普罗瑟表示，如果电影的故事设定在某个特定的地点，那么戏服能够反映当地生长的植物会更加真实。在英国，柳条会很合适，而在西班牙，则适合使用西班牙草（Esparto grass）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "邓克利及其团队利用斯卡斯加德的3D模型进行工作，以确保“观众能够认出篮子形态的亚历山大”。这其中的关键在于邓克利所称的“斯卡斯加德式忧郁眼神”，他们通过确保编织层能够在眉毛处起皱来实现这一点。他的头发、胡须和睫毛都是用新西兰亚麻的纤维（muka）制成的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "邓克利将来自编织社群的关注和批评形容为“真的很酷”，他表示：“我并不怪任何人。真正的工艺大师为之奉献了多年。我完全预料到他们会审视自己艺术形式的奇幻版本并挑出毛病。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于柳条纯粹主义者，摩根表示电影中“不乏与柳条相关的视觉盛宴”，她指出了大量的编篮场景。普罗瑟表示，他对该片能够引起人们对编篮工艺的关注感到兴奋，特别是现在一些技能和传统工艺已经面临濒危。TikTok上充斥着藤编戏服制作指南，其中包括斯卡斯加德称之为戏服“最棒部分”的乳头道具教程。他将自己的一对道具送给了电视节目主持人格雷厄姆·诺顿（Graham Norton），并形容其为“非凡的工艺”。", "links": [{"text": "skills and traditional techniques are now endangered", "url": "https://basketmakersassociation.org.uk/traditional-basketry-project/"}, {"text": "TV host Graham Norton", "url": "https://www.youtube.com/shorts/5QKxRIYx2MY"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Film", "links": [{"text": "Film", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/film"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Craft", "links": [{"text": "Craft", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/craft"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Alexander Skarsgård", "links": [{"text": "Alexander Skarsgård", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/alexander-skarsgard"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Textile art", "links": [{"text": "Textile art", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/culture/textile-art"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Visual effects (VFX)", "links": [{"text": "Visual effects (VFX)", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/visual-effects"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "news", "links": [{"text": "news", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tone/news"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
Hollywood heart-throbs are known for their good looks and charisma. But in a classic plot twist, the latest big-screen dreamboat causing viewers to get hot and bothered isn’t even human.

Alexander Skarsgård’s Wicker Husband character in the romcom Wicker has sent the internet into a frenzy.

“Never looking at my patio furniture the same again,” says one Instagram comment. Ikea captioned a picture of its wicker furniture with the term “husband material”.

The basketweaving community, however, is getting worked up for very different reasons. The fact the Wicker Husband isn’t made of willow, and he appears to be plaited rather than woven, has angered some makers.

Deborah Needleman, former editor of the New York Times’s T magazine turned basket maker, was one of the first to question it. Writing on Instagram , she said: “I’m excited that the basketweaving community now has our own hot, woven leading man, but I’ve also got issues. Why is a dude woven in an English fishing village not made of willow – or even rush?!” More than 100 fellow basket makers have since weighed in.

The Oxford English dictionary defines wicker as “thin sticks of wood twisted together to make baskets, furniture etc”.

Eleanor Morgan, trade adviser to the Worshipful Company of Basketmakers in London, says that while willow has commonly been used to denote wicker, it is less popular today. “Historically wicker could have meant any pliant twig or osier,” she says.

Joe Dunckley, a prosthetic designer at Wētā workshop, the special effects studio in New Zealand that created the upper body of the Wicker Husband, says it was a “big challenge” to create a costume for a character that is sentient but made of wicker. “Most prosthetic materials are soft to mimic skin. But he’s not flesh and bone.”

To get the wicker effect, Dunckley and his team of 80 specialists created 50 interlocking body pieces for Skarsgård to wear. Using a rubber-like thermoplastic elastomer, they were able to 3D print a bespoke weave coded by the studio that was then attached to a spandex suit. During the 18-month process they also created 10 facial appliances.

Dunckley says willow wasn’t a viable option for what they needed the suit to be able to do. “It is a similar reason to why, in film, we don’t make armour out of actual steel or use real swords. This is a fantasy film.”

Lewis Prosser, a basket maker from Cardiff, says every maker is thinking about how they would have approached the task. “It certainly isn’t the way I would have done it, but that doesn’t mean that it is bad,” he says.

Prosser says his understanding of wicker is that it is “an object that is woven but one that is specifically not textile”, adding that “some will disagree with me”. Some basket makers, including Needleman, argue that wicker refers to a type of weave rather than a material.

after newsletter promotion

For Prosser, who creates wicker costumes using techniques traditionally found in Wales and the south-west of England, there are three main ways to make a basket. Coiling, where threads of plant materials are wound together in a spiral, braiding, or stake and stand basketry whereby vertical rods are woven through horizontal strands. “What we would traditionally call ‘wicker items’ would usually have that latter aspect,” Prosser says. The Wicker Husband does not.

Although the actor Olivia Colman and her fellow villagers in the film speak in a range of British dialects, the film is not set in England. Dunckley suggests the basket maker character played by Peter Dinklage has travelled the world, learning skills from other makers.

Prosser says that if the film had been set in a specific location, it would be more authentic for the costume to reflect the plants that grow there. In the UK, willow would be apt, whereas in Spain, Esparto grass would be fitting.

Dunckley and his team worked using a 3D cast of Skarsgård to ensure the “audience would be able to recognise Alexander in basket form”. Key to this is what Dunckley calls the “Skarsgård smoulder”, which they captured by ensuring the weave could furrow at the brow. His hair, beard and lashes were made from muka, fibres from New Zealand flax.

Describing the interest and criticism from the weaving community as “really cool”, Dunckley says: “I don’t blame anyone. True artists of the craft have dedicated years to it. I would expect them to look at a fantasy version of their art form and see failings in it.”

For the willow purists, Morgan says “there is no lack of osier-related eye candy” in the film, pointing to a plethora of basket scenes. Prosser says he is thrilled the film has drawn attention to basket making, especially as some skills and traditional techniques are now endangered . TikTok is rife with wicker costume making guides, including nipple tutorials which Skarsgård has said was the “best part” of his suit. He gave his own pair to the TV host Graham Norton describing them as “extraordinary craftsmanship”.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Darren Lynn Bousman , a filmmaker known for his work across the Saw horror franchise, has come aboard to direct Serpentine , a new thriller from Dream State Studios and partner Brand in Entertainment .

Serpentine is set in a seemingly quiet New England town where organized crime, crooked cops, buried secrets and the intensely competitive world of figure skating begin to collide.

At the center of the film is a woman who believes she has found a way out of a dangerous life, only to discover that escape comes with consequences. What begins as an attempt to disappear quickly pulls her into a strange web of criminals, local power players, and people with their own reasons for keeping the past buried.

Bousman told Deadline, “I’ve wanted for a long time to flex some different muscles outside of the horror genre, and SERPENTINE gives me that opportunity without completely abandoning the things I love. There’s still dread, fear and a real sense of intensity running through it, but it exists in this strange, darkly funny, FARGO-esque world that feels very different from anything I’ve directed before. That combination is what really excites me.”

Watch on Deadline

Valerie Palencar, President of Dream State Studios and writer of Serpentine , said, “Darren immediately understood what makes SERPENTINE unusual. This is a story driven by complex characters operating in a world where ambition and loyalty are constantly being tested. Darren has an extraordinary ability to create tension while never losing sight of character, and we are enormously excited to have him directing the film.”

Serpentine is being produced by Dream State Studios, with Brand in Entertainment CEO Rolfe J. Auerbach executive producing. The film will be funded partly by brands, brought in by Brand in Entertainment, whose products have been integrated into the story from the earliest stages.

“SERPENTINE was never intended to be a conventional independent film,” said Auerbach. “We are building a commercially ambitious motion picture around an extraordinary story, an internationally recognized director and a financing model that brings major consumer brands directly into the world of the film. Darren gives SERPENTINE exactly the combination of intensity, originality and commercial filmmaking experience we were looking for.”

A filmmaker who has worked in both the studio and independent spaces, Bousman is best known for directing four Saw films, beginning with 2005’s Saw II , which marked his feature debut. The others were Saw III , Saw IV and the Chris Rock spin-off Spiral: From the Book of Saw . He co-wrote Saw II with Leigh Whannell and is otherwise known for projects like Repo! The Genetic Opera , The Devil’s Carnival , Abattoir and Death of Me . He’s represented by Verve, Wonder Street, and Skrzyniarz and Mallean.

article_text:
The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival opened Monday with a rain-soaked red carpet and a ceremony at Hulic Hall, where Japan’s government used the occasion to restate its goal of selling JPY20 trillion ($133 billion) worth of Japanese content overseas by 2033.

The festival received 1,892 film submissions from 112 countries and regions this year. It opened with “Sukiyaki,” which tells how the title tune was written and went on to top the U.S. Billboard chart in 1963. Director Zeze Takahisa took the stage with Okada Junichi, who plays composer Nakamura Hachidai, Matsuzaka Tori, who plays lyricist Ei Rokusuke, and Seino Nana, who plays Nakamura Junko.

Zeze said the film is set in the years after the war, as Japan entered its period of rapid economic growth, and that its founding idea is the war itself and how the characters come to think about what peace means. “Through this film, I hope this festival, too, can become a festival of peace,” he said.

Popular on Variety

Matsuzaka said the shoot began in April last year and that the film had taken a little over a year to reach audiences. “It isn’t just about enjoying the music. It’s a film where you can feel the live energy, as if you were actually in the venue,” he said.

Seino said she had watched her co-stars’ stage performances from the audience seats during filming. “Seeing everyone’s souls colliding, going beyond their roles, really moved me,” she said.

In a video message played during the ceremony, Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae said her cabinet has designated content, including film, as a strategic priority under its Japan growth strategy, with public-private domestic investment set to accelerate. To reach the 2033 target, the government plans production support for Japanese films and efforts to attract foreign location shoots.

“Film has the power to connect people’s hearts across countries and regions, and to deepen understanding of diverse cultures and values,” Takaichi said.

Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Akazawa Ryosei said overseas sales of Japanese content have already grown to around JPY6.1 trillion ($40.7 billion), and that the government has sought roughly JPY250 billion ($1.67 billion) across ministries in its fiscal 2027 budget request to support growth investment in the content industry.

Akazawa pointed to the fifth “Kingdom” film, which made the franchise the first series in film history to see five consecutive installments pass JPY5 billion ($33 million) at the box office, with a cumulative gross above JPY30 billion ($200 million). He also noted that the festival’s Centerpiece film, “Godzilla Minus Zero,” the follow-up to Oscar visual effects winner “Godzilla Minus One,” will open worldwide next month, including in Japan, Asia and North America.

Festival director Hisamatsu Takeo, who said he is approaching 50 years in the film business, thanked guests for turning out in bad weather before declaring the festival open. “There are so many kinds of film in the world, each with its own appeal and its own way of being enjoyed,” Hisamatsu said. “Nothing would make me happier than sharing the appeal of such diverse and varied cinema with all of you and enjoying it together.”

Filmmaker Rolf de Heer , president of the competition jury, which also includes actor Watanabe Makiko, DI colorist Yov Moor and producers Oh Jungwan and Alex Lo, recalled seeing an Ozu film more than 50 years ago. “I still remember one shot, so perfect. And Oshima, and of course Kurosawa. ‘Dersu Uzala’ is in my brain,” de Heer said. “So we as the jury are very privileged to be able to work in the country of those masters.”

Actor and singer Nakajima Kento, serving as TIFF Navigator, said walking the carpet carried a special sense of occasion. “It was raining today, but I felt it was a blessing of rain that would help the future of film flourish even more,” he said.

Among those on the carpet were director Milcho Manchevski and the cast of “Sister Brother Manhole Cover,” including Sara Klimoska, on her third visit to Tokyo. Director Qiu Jiongjiong led the cast of “Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting,” Indonesian auteur Garin Nugroho the “Red Before Dawn” team, and Tadanobu Asano, Sode Yukiko and cast members represented “Only Lovers in the Night.”

Judy Ongg represented “Sunshine Women’s Choir,” a gala selection title billed by TIFF as Taiwan’s No. 1 hit. Ongg won best actress at the seventh Taiwan Film Critics Society Awards, was nominated for best supporting actress at the 28th Taipei Film Awards and is nominated in the same category at the upcoming 63rd Golden Horse Awards.

The carpet also welcomed Academy CEO Bill Kramer, Academy president Lynette Howell Taylor and chief membership, impact and industry officer Meredith Shea, who are in Tokyo for TIFF’s Academy in Tokyo program.

“This is the first time the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has participated at the Tokyo film festival. To be part of such a major platform as the Tokyo International Film Festival makes this especially meaningful, and we feel honored to be here,” Kramer said.

article_text:
T his gloomy-toned film takes its sweet time revealing its genre nature, emerging as a proper horror flick more than halfway in with a detailed transformation sequence. It’s the sort of showreel stuff that special effects technicians and aficionados revel in, although others might find the creature design a little plasticky, not unlike the things we see being 3D-printed elsewhere in the feature.

It’s a shame that the hardcore creature-feature stuff is a letdown because the drama leading up to it isn’t bad. We start with a forensic science expert called Meg (Deborah Ann Woll), a young woman whose shiny hair and perky professional attitude disguises a steely composure and strong stomach that’s not in the slightest bit discombobulated by all the rotting, decomposing flesh she deals with on the daily.

Meg is not in the least upset, or so it seems, when one of the bodies found at a murder site is revealed by DNA tests to be that of her own father, Peter (played in flashbacks by David Myers Gregory), who went missing when Meg was but a girl. Nor is she hesitant to pick up her scalpel and commence an autopsy on Dad’s corpse, finding strange anomalies on his anatomy, including evidence of gunshots and multiple ribs that broke and healed over the years. Father and son police officers Marks (Jeffrey Donovan) and Ian (Will Hochman) look on aghast but sort of impressed.

The mystery deepens further when the facility containing the bodies burns down. Meg and her cop colleagues start to uncover hitherto little known connections between Peter and the circumstances of his disappearance and a couple of locals. Meg even starts to suspect that her mother (Gretchen Corbett) hasn’t been telling her the whole truth about her dad’s doings before he went missing, and their mother and child co-dependent tendency to never speak of the missing starts to look like a rubbish way to deal with trauma. But all the sticky, intriguing psychological stuff gets backburnered when it’s time for the howling and hunting to start.

英国出身でニューヨークを拠点に活動する写真家、フィル・ペンマン（Phil Penman）の個展「The Unwritten Stage 〜名もなき舞台」が、2026年11月26日（木）から2027年2月7日（日）まで、東京・銀座のライカギャラリー東京で開催される。

25年以上にわたりニューヨークのストリートを撮影してきたペンマンは、鮮明なコントラストと緻密な構図を特徴とする写真家。『The Guardian』『National Geographic』『TIME』などで作品を発表し、2001年のアメリカ同時多発テロ事件後の記録は9/11 Memorial & Museumに、コロナ禍のロックダウン下で撮影した作品は米国議会図書館に収蔵されている。

本展では、写真集『New York Street Diaries』『Street Scenes』から作品を紹介。街角で行き交う人々の表情や仕草、光と影が交差する都市の風景を通して、名もなき人々の日常に潜む物語を浮かび上がらせる。

ペンマンは自身の撮影について、「私にとって大切なのは、忍耐である。訪れる瞬間を予測し、フレームの幾何学を組み立て、そこへ物語が歩み入るのを待つ」と語る。雨や雪などの悪天候も積極的に受け入れながら、都市と人間が一瞬だけ調和する瞬間を捉えてきた。

見知らぬ人々の存在感と、絶えず変化する都市の表情。ニューヨークをひとつの舞台に見立て、日常のなかにある一度きりの情景を描き出す展覧会となる。

article_text:
More than 45 years after the first Friday the 13th , Brad Caleb Kane is righting a wrong from the set of the 1980 slasher.

Ahead of Friday’s Crystal Lake premiere on Peacock , the series creator noted to Deadline that a snake Pamela Voorhees (Linda Cardellini) sets free after finding it in the camp pantry in the first episode is “a direct nod” to a trained serpent that was actually killed while filming the original movie.

“But [Pam’s] a different person in the first episode than the kids are [in the movie],” he explained. “Yes, it’s a direct nod, but then it goes to the place of the first movie.”

Kane clarified: “But we don’t actually kill a snake in ours. No, no animals were harmed in the making of Crystal Lake . Some hippies might have been harmed in the making of Crystal Lake , but no animals.”

Watch on Deadline

During the filming of the original 1980 slasher Friday the 13th , a domesticated bull snake was infamously killed in real life while shooting the scene in which “final girl” Alice (Adrienne King) finds the reptile slithering around her cabin and calls for her fellow counselors to come help.

In the scene, Bill (Harry Crosby) runs in with a machete and kills the snake, before it’s shown writhing and dying on the floor. Cast and crew have since revealed that the sequence was real , noting that the snake’s handler was unaware of the film’s intentions and was “inconsolable” afterward.

With PETA launching two months before Friday the 13th ‘s premiere in 1980, there were no animal protection laws in place yet during the filming of the Sean S. Cunningham-helmed movie.

Streaming Friday on Peacock, Crystal Lake stars Linda Cardellini as Pam Voorhees, who struggles to grieve after her son Jason drowned the summer before. As two strangers begin digging into her mysterious past, Pam goes to murderous lengths to keep her secrets buried.
